description: Space NUTS is a Perth-based team combining GIS, remote sensing, geospatial technology and geoscience backgrounds.
summary:
NISAR Change Explorer turns NASA-ISRO radar observations into evidence that people can explore, compare and use to plan further checks. Designed for users without specialist radar knowledge, the web app brings eight cases of water, farmland, fire and a landslide into one interactive map.

Users compare radar changes over time with optical imagery and official records, inspect values and available time series, and see where observations agree or differ. In supported cases, they can adjust a rule, highlight candidate areas and export them to GIS with the selection criteria attached. At Sale Common wetland, a radar rule selected 72% of cells labelled as new water in optical imagery, while selecting about 5% of stable-land reference cells.

The app makes both the evidence and its limits visible, helping users identify where a closer look is needed. Its open, reusable workflow can be extended to new locations and longer time series. With further field validation and user testing, it could support routine wetland monitoring, agricultural change assessment and post-fire inspections.
details:
NISAR Change Explorer is an interactive web application for investigating land-surface change using NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band radar. It brings eight cases covering water, farmland, fire and a landslide into a common analytical workflow, helping users explore observations, compare evidence and identify locations that warrant further investigation.

Users can compare radar images and change maps across dates, switch between HH and HV polarisations, and consult available optical imagery and official records. Clicking a radar-image location or a supported farm field reveals its time series; clicking an analysis cell displays its change values and reference labels. In the Sale Common and Rockadooie cases, users can adjust selection rules, inspect the highlighted candidates and export them as GeoJSON with the selection criteria attached.

We use NISAR Level 2 Geocoded Polarimetric Covariance products distributed by the Alaska Satellite Facility. The analysis matches acquisitions by track and frame, applies product quality information to screen the data, and summarises observations at appropriate spatial scales. Radar power is averaged in the linear domain before conversion to decibels; inputs already expressed in decibels are not converted again. Each change is interpreted against an appropriate reference, such as a preceding observation interval, stable land or the surrounding landscape. Sentinel-2 imagery, river gauges, rainfall records, official burn boundaries and Copernicus emergency mapping provide complementary evidence.

The case studies demonstrate different uses of this approach:

  • At Sale Common wetland, areas identified as new water in optical imagery generally corresponded to decreases in radar backscatter, while areas where water receded showed increases. The app presents these relationships spatially and lets users explore how different selection rules affect the results.
  • In Burdekin farmland, field C showed declines in both optical greenness and radar backscatter, with median HH and HV changes of −7.63 and −11.22 dB. Other fields showed differing optical and radar responses, demonstrating the value of examining both observations rather than assuming that they will agree.
  • At Rockadooie, median HH backscatter increased by approximately 2.63 dB inside the official burn boundary, compared with approximately 1.2 dB in the surrounding comparison areas. We present this spatial contrast alongside the burn record and optical changes to inform the selection of locations for post-burn checks.
  • At Timure, the app brings together radar changes across the landslide, a longer observation record and Copernicus-mapped impact. This supports retrospective examination of the event and its surface response. We do not report ground displacement from products that failed quality checks.

The project's creative contribution is the connection between interactive exploration, evidence comparison and transparent selection rules. Users can examine what supports an interpretation, where observations differ, and how adjusting a threshold changes the candidate areas. Exported results retain their selection criteria, allowing subsequent analysis to be traced back to the rule that produced them. This is intended to help land and water managers, researchers and GIS users plan further observations and field checks.

The Timure case also reflects a personal concern for project lead Qing Ding. After hearing accounts of the suffering caused by the disaster, Qing wanted to use this project to explore whether observable changes might precede sudden failures, and whether sustained observation could help us recognise signals that are currently missed or poorly understood.

That concern extends to glaciers and other unstable mountain terrain. We hope to combine longer, quality-controlled satellite time series with field measurements and geological and meteorological information to investigate whether gradual deformation or other surface anomalies can provide meaningful early indications of instability. Satellite observations cannot directly measure internal stress in a slope. The deformation products available for this project did not meet the quality requirements for reliable analysis in the source area, so we have not established evidence suitable for pre-event warning. This remains a research question requiring further investigation and validation.

The current product is a case-study prototype. Differences in acquisition timing, spatial resolution, data quality and processing versions affect interpretation. Next steps include validating candidate areas against field and farm records, testing the application with users, and extending the workflow to more locations and longer time series. With further validation, potential applications include routine wetland monitoring, agricultural change assessment and post-fire inspections. Any application to early warning would require specific validation of the relationship between observed anomalies and subsequent events.

The application uses Python, rasterio, NumPy, Pillow and Shapely for processing, and HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Leaflet for the interface. It is hosted on GitHub Pages and uses an OpenStreetMap base map. Cases are organised through configuration files to support reuse, and the project code is released under the Apache License 2.0.
